No, do not approve the plan to scale immediately to $1,000 a day. 

While the current 3.2 ROAS looks strong, that metric relies on a blended attribution window that often overstates platform-reported revenue. More importantly, surging spend to $30,000 a month against a strict inventory ceiling of 4,000 bottles creates severe stockout and cash-flow risks. At $1,000 daily, inventory would deplete in roughly 130 days, but holiday traffic compression will accelerate that velocity, leading to stockouts before your 10-week manufacturing lead time allows a replenishment batch to arrive.

Instead, run a phased spend plan. Maintain a conservative daily budget of $400 through October to preserve inventory, then scale to $600 daily in November to capture early holiday demand without exhausting stock prematurely. Reserve the remainder for targeted retargeting and high-converting holiday windows in December. 

This approach assumes your current 3.2 ROAS will experience diminishing marginal returns as you scale spend threefold. It also prioritizes retaining enough inventory to service high-margin 90-day reorders, protecting your customer lifetime value. 

Approve the aggressive $1,000-a-day plan only if two criteria are met: first, you immediately issue a rush manufacturing order to cover holiday volume, and second, your blended contribution margin after variable costs and platform fees exceeds the point where lower marginal ROAS at scale still yields a net profit. If you cannot guarantee expedited manufacturing, stick to the phased budget to protect cash flow and prevent stockouts during peak selling season.
